Ultrasonography

Sorin M. Dudea

Ultrasonography – or ultrasound – represents a group of examination methods, mainly based on images, that use, as a vector of medical information, ultrasound (US) reflflected within the human body.

5.1. Basic acoustics

5.1.1. Definition of sound

Sound is a vibration of matter transmitted as mechanical waves by solid, liquid or gaseous media particles.

A particle of the respective environment must vibrate for a mechanical wave to appear, yielding energy to the neighboring particles. The initial particle that vibrates and induces the emergence of the wave is called the wave source, and in the case of sound – the sound source. The waves consist of condensation areas (compression) that regularly alternate with dissipation areas (decompression) of the transmission medium particles. Sounds are mechanical waves. Unlike electromagnetic waves, which propagate in vacuum, a material environment is required to propagate sound.

The wave can be graphically represented as a sinusoidal curve (fifigure 22) consisting of a succession of positive and negative oscillations, symmetrical to a baseline.

5.1.2. Characteristics of sound waves

The physical quantities that characterize sound waves are (fifigure 22):

  • the amplitude (A) defifines the maxi- mum displacement of the particle in one direction or another from the baseline po- sition;

Fig. 22. Graphic representation of the sound wave: A = amplitude; T = period; λ = wavelength.

­ the period (T) represents the time required for the particle to perform a complete oscillation and return to the initial baseline position, moving in the same direction. The period is measured in seconds. As a physical measure, the period is inversely related to the frequency (T = 1 / F);

­ the wavelength (λ) represents the distance covered by the sound wave during the period. Wavelength is measured in metric units;

­ the frequency (F) represents the number of complete oscillations in the unit of time (second). The unit of measurement for frequency is HERTZ (Hz).

1 Hz = 1 oscillation / second

The multiples of this unit of measurement are kilohertz: 1 kHz = 1000 Hz and megahertz: 1 MHz = 1,000,000 Hz.

Depending on their frequency, the sound waves may be divided into infrasound (0-16 Hz), audible sound (16 Hz – 18 kHz) and ultrasound (US) (18 kHz – 150 MHz).

The ultrasound waves used in the ultrasound diagnosis usually have a frequency between 3 – 18 MHz.

­ the speed (c) of sound represents the distance covered by the wave in the unit of time. It is measured in meters/second. The formula that gives the relation with the other parameters of the sound wave is:

c = F × λ

The speed of sound propagation in a homogeneous environment is constant at a given temperature and depends on the environment’s characteristics. The speed of sound is low in gases, higher in liquids and even higher in solid media.

For diagnostic ultrasonography, an ave- rage value of 1540 m/sec was set as the reference level for US propagation speed in the human body’s soft tissues. The microprocessor of any ultrasound machine uses this

As the speed of sound in a given environment is constant, the frequency and wavelength of sound passing through that material are inversely proportional;

­ the acoustic energy. Sound waves are variations in the pressure exerted on the particles of an environment. The acoustic source generates an amount of energy, which determines the compression/decompression of the environment. This energy is transmitted jointly with the wave. The wave energy is measured in joules (J). For each sound wave, according to the energy, one may defifine intensity and power.

5.1.3. Genesis of ultrasound 5.1.3.1. The piezoelectric effect. The

piezoelectric effect generates the ultrasound waves used in ultrasonography. This physical effect is specifific only to certain materials, called piezoelectric materials, their prototype being the quartz crystal. This effect describes certain materials’ ability to generate an electric charge in response to applied mechanical stress. When an electric charge is applied to a piezoelectric material, it undergoes mechanical deformation, followed by US emission. Conversely, the mechanical deformation of a piezoelectric material when hit by US leads to an electric charge’s appearance.

5.1.3.2. ThThe acoustic source is the initial material point that vibrates and from which sound propagates. The instrument that emits US waves in the human body, acting both as a sound source and a sound receiver, is called a transducer. The transducer is the device held by the examiner’s hand during US scanning. 28 l I. INTRODUCTORY NOTIONS

5.1.3.3. The ultrasound pulse. In

ultrasonography, the same piezoelectric device emits the US and receives the echoes. Transmission and reception are performed alternately: the transducer emits a short burst of US (pulse), after which, for some time, it receives the echoes, thus performing the pulse-echo cycle. This cycle is repeated rhythmically.

The pulse-echo cycle comprises two components: the drive pulse of US and the echo reception period (fifigure 23). The pulse repetition frequency (PRF) defifines the number of pulses (pulse-echo cycles) produced by the transducer in one second. The PRF measurement unit is Hz, and the usual size of PRF is kHz. Spatial pulse length (SPL) defifines the distance covered by the wave during an US pulse production.

5.1.3.4. Qualities of piezoelectric

materials. The emitted sound duration defifines the capacity of resonance of a piezoelectric material after a single electrical stimulus. Very short US pulses are used in the ultrasound diagnosis to obtain the best possible image quality. For this, the transducers are built of piezoelectric synthetic ceramics. These materials are both costly and very fragile (like porcelain).

Fig. 23. Representation of the pulse-echo cycle of the US transducer. The emitted US burst (pulse) is folowed by the US reception period.

5.1.3.5. The resonant frequency of the

transducer represents the frequency of the US emitted while the conversion of electric energy into acoustic energy is achieved with maximum effificiency. The resonant frequency of a ceramic device depends on the thickness of the ceramic. The thicker the material, the lower the emitted US frequency. Due to the thickness dependence of the piezoelectric material, the nominal frequency is predetermined during the transducer’s manufacture and has a fifixed value for each transducer. The transducer emits the US not only at the resonant frequency but also at its harmonics. Electrical stimulation of the piezoelectric material results in a spectrum of ultrasonic frequencies, in which those with the value of the resonant frequency dominate.

5.1.3 .6. ThThe ultrasound beam. When an electrical stimulus is applied to a piece of piezoelectric material, a beam (or bundle) of US is emitted from the material’s entire surface. The US beam thickness is not uniform, being determined primarily by the piezoelectric material’s diameter. Near the ceramic surface, the US beam has a cylindrical shape and a tapered shape in the remote region.

5.1.4. Acoustic properties of tissues

Biological tissues have several properties that inflfluence their interaction with ultrasonic waves.

The speed of ultrasound propaga­

tion is a constant characteristic for each tissue. It varies within relatively small limits for different types of soft tissues.

Elasticity is the body’s property to return to its original shape and volume after being subjected to mechanical deformation.

Stiffness defifines the resistance of a material to compression. For parenchymal organs, stiffness depends on the proportion of fifibrous connective tissue that contributes to the organ structure. Stiffness is the main factor that determines the speed of sound propagation in a tissue. The higher the stiffness, the higher the propagation speed.

Density defifines the concentration of matter and expresses mass/unit volume.

Acoustic impedance (Z) is a quantity that defifines the extent to which an environment allows the propagation of ultrasound. It is calculated by the product of the sound speed through a given medium and the density of that medium. The acoustic impedances of the soft tissues in the human body have very close values, while air and bone are characterized by values that deviate far from the average for soft tissues. Acoustic impedance values are of great importance in the generation of reflflected ultrasound.

5.2. US behavior in the human body

5.2.1. US waves propagate linearly in biological tissues. Inside the human body, ultrasonic waves emitted by a transducer be- have similarly to a light beam. They undergo the effects of transmission, reflflection, refraction and diffraction phenomena and other specifific US phenomena such as attenuation, absorption and diffusion.

5.2.2. Ultrasound transmission and

reflflection. The notion of interface defifines, in ultrasound, the separation surface between two environments with different acoustic impedanc- es. When an US beam encounters an interface, some of the incident beam’s energy is reflflected, returning to the source environment in the form of reflflected US waves and generating the echo that underlies the ultrasound diagnosis. The incident beam’s

5. ULTRASONOGRAPHY l 29 remaining energy is transmitted into the second environment, where it will undergo new phenomena of reflflection and transmission (fifigure 24).

The amounts of reflflected and transmitted US energy are inversely proportional.

At the interface between any soft tissue and air or bone, US is totally reflflected due to the signifificant differences of acoustic impedance between environments. Consequently, no US is transmitted distal to the interface. In the absence of transmitted US, no echoes are returned and medical information completely lacks.

Both air and bone prevent the transmission of US and therefore make US examina- tion impossible.

Fig. 24. Transmission and reflflection of US at the level of an interface. Details in the text. 30 l I. INTRODUCTORY NOTIONS

5.2.3. Beam scattering defifines the dispersion of US as clutter, low amplitude echoes when the beam interacts with irregular surface structures. Dispersion is the basis for the appearance of scattering echoes – the phenomenon of ultrasonic scintillation – which are of signifificant importance in generating the ultrasound image. These echoes’ occurrence depends not only on the angle of incidence of the primary US beam but also on the quantity and quality of interference between secondary US waves. Scattering echoes play an essential role in generating the ultrasound image of the parenchymal organs.

5.2.4. Absorption defifines the gradual loss of energy of the incident beam, during propagation, by the gradual transformation of acoustic energy into thermal energy.

5.2.5. Ultrasonic beam attenuation represents the sum of acoustic energy losses resulting from absorption, scattering and reflflection. Typically only 20% of sound energy is lost through dispersion and reflflection. The factors that inflfluence the attenuation are:

  • absorption determines 80% of energy los- ses;
  • dispersion plays an important role in atte- nuation if there are a large number of small interfaces with dimensions close to λ (e.g., adipose or fifibrous tissue);
  • - reflflection has a role in attenuation, especi- ally in the presence of highly reflflective interfaces (e.g., air, bone, stones, ba- rium);
  • -distancecovered.Attenuationisanexponential phenomenon, being proportional to the square of the distance covered by the US beam;
  • - US frequency. Attenuation is directly pro- portional to the frequency of the US beam. High-frequency ultrasound is attenuated quickly after a short distan- ce and only low-frequency US is trans- mitted in depth.

5.2.6. The US beam penetration

capacity defifines the distance from the transducer to the farthest point where the transmitted beam intensity is still suffificient to generate echoes useful for diagnosis. In other words, an US beam’s penetration capacity defifines the depth to which that beam allows ultrasound exploration. As with the reflflection-transmission relationship, penetration is the antagonistic term for attenuation.

5.3. Obtaining and graphically recording the ultrasonographic information

5.3.1. The fundamental principle of obtaining ultrasonic information

Classical ultrasound techniques, which produce anatomical information, analyze the intensity of the echo. The transducer alternately functions as an US transmitter and receiver. The US emission has, therefore, a pulsating, intermittent character. As it propagates in the transmission medium, the emitted US pulse encounters interfaces. Part of the acoustic energy is reflflected at each interface level, generating echoes, and the rest is transmitted further to another interface. The echoes cover the incident beam’s reverse path, interact with the transducer and generate electrical impulses through the piezoelectric effect. The echo corresponding to the interface closest to the transducer is received fifirst. After that, echoes from more and more distant interfaces are received later and later.

Following the emission of a single US pulse, multiple echoes are received, separated in time, due to the spacing of the interfaces that generated them (fifigure 25).

5.4. Modalities of graphical representation of the ultrasonic information

All echoes received after the emission of a single US pulse form a line of ultrasono- graphic information. The electrical pulses corresponding to the received echoes can be displayed graphically in several ways.

5.4.4. Real­time examination.

The transducer consists of one or more crystals of piezoelectric material, mechanically driven or electronically activated successively. The examiner keeps the transducer still on the patient’s skin. The piezoelectric crystals generate a rapid succession of ultrasound images (up to 60 images/ sec.), displayed successively, at the same fast rate, on the scanner monitor. The result is a “fifilm” of the examined structures, which shows their movement. This technique is currently used in all clinical applications of ultrasonographic diagnosis.

5.5. The ultrasound image

The fifinal product of any ultrasonographic examination is the ultrasound image. The ultrasound diagnosis is based on this image.

5.5.1. The structure of the ultrasound image

An ultrasound image consists of all the ultrasonic information lines obtained after performing, with the transducer, a single sweeping movement on the area of interest. The ultrasound image is a digital image, where the information is converted into the binary system and stored in a computer’s memory.

The image displayed on the monitor consists of multiple small square elements, called pixels (picture element). Each pixel corresponds to a cell of the matrix that forms the digital memory.

5.5.2. Resolution

In medical imaging, the term resolution, generally used, defifines the detail that an image or method provides. The more numerous the details, the better the resolution. In ultrasonography, resolution is defifined from three points of view: detail resolution, contrast resolution and temporal resolution. of the image). 5.5.2.1. ThThe detail resolution defifines the minimum distance between two different points in space that appear separately on the ultrasound image. The smaller the dis- tance between the two points, the better the resolution.

The detail resolution is measured in millimeters. If the distance between two interfaces is greater than the resolution’s numerical value, the two interfaces determine, on the ultrasound image, two separate echoes. If the distance between interfaces is less than the resolution value, a single thick, irregular echo appears on the ultrasound image instead of two interfaces. The main factors that determine the resolution are the US frequency and the US beam thickness. To obtain good quality ultrasound images, it is necessary to use high-frequency US (7.5-15 MHz) and thin US beams ( focused).

5.5.2.2. The contrast resolution de-

fifines the machine’s ability to discriminate between echoes with identical sizes but different intensities. This discrimination is done using the gray level scale on the image.

5.5.2.3. Temporal resolution defifines the ability of the method to represent rapidly unfolding events over time. M-mode ultrasound is considered a high temporal resolution technique, as one of its dimensions is time.

For real-time two-dimensional ultrasound, the determining factor of the temporal resolution is the number of images generated and displayed on the monitor in one second, respectively, the frequency of the images (frame rate). The higher the image frequency, the better the temporal resolution.

5.5.3. Ultrasound image format

The constructive features of the transducer determine the format of the ultrasound image. The format can be rectangular (linear transducers), the triangular shape of a circle sector (sector transducers), double-sided trapezoidal-shaped arcs (convex transducers), or circular (endocavitary transducers) (fifigure 29).

5.6. Specific terminology in ultrasound exploration

Ultrasonography uses its own terms that describe the aspects encountered in the image. The most commonly used terms are:

  • transonic or anechogenic – any structure without echoes (non-image), which appears on the image as black and which most often denotes the liquid consistency of a region (fifigure 30);
  • echogenic – structure that strongly re- flflects the US, appears white on the image and can be produced by connec- tive tissue structures, bone, calcifificati- ons, stones, air, metal, etc. (fifigure 31);
  • echostructure – the totality of the echo- es produced by a parenchymal tissue, organized in a coherent structure that allows the identifification and characte- rization of the examined organ (fifigure 32);
  • hyper – or hypoechoic – terms used when comparing the intensity of echoes pro- duced by the examined organ/structu- re to a reference organ/structure;

5.7. Doppler effect

5.7.1. Definition

The Doppler effect, described by Christian Doppler in 1842, defifines the received wavelength’s behavior when the source of the wave and the receiver of the wave are in relative motion (to each other). According to this effect, three distinct situations may be encountered: tructure. Normal testis. ciated to a gallstone.

  • if the source of the wave is stationary with respect to the receiver, λ (implicitly also the frequency) of the received wave is equal to λ (and the frequency) of the transmitted wave;
  • if the source of the wave and the receiver are closing in, received λ is smaller (implicitly the received frequency is higher) than that of the transmitted wave;
  • if the source of the wave and the receiver move away, the received λ is greater (implicitly, the received frequency is lower) than that of the transmitted wave.

The Doppler effect is common to all types of waves, regardless of their nature. It is used in radio astronomy to study astral bodies’ movement using electromagnetic waves and industry or medicine, where applications primarily concern sound waves. Doppler-based radars are used in meteorology as well as aviation and car traffific monitoring. Electronic home alarms or automatic door openers also use the Doppler effect.

5.7.2. Application of the Doppler effect in medical diagnosis – physical principles

In the human body, the reflflector or «target» studied using the Doppler effect is the blood flflow in the heart and vessels, characterized by direction and movement speed. Doppler ultrasonography studies the frequency of echoes as opposed to twodimensional ultrasound, where the echoes’ intensity encodes anatomical information.

If one considers two transducers placed side by side on an anatomical region, one of which continually emits US with a known and constant emission frequency (EF) and the other continually receives echoes with variable reflflected frequency (RF), depending on the direction of move-

5. ULTRASONOGRAPHY l 37 ment of the reflflector (blood flflow, the „target” reflflecting the US), the following situations may be encountered, according to the Doppler effect:

  • if the reflflector is stationary: RF = EF;
  • if the reflflector (blood flflow) approaches the transducer: RF>EF;
  • if the reflflector (blood flflow) moves away from the transducer: RF<EF.

Frequency variation or differential fre- quency (DF) is the difference between the reflflected and the emitted frequency. DF is the basic information obtained by Doppler examination and it is named Doppler shift. It is calculated by the formula:

DF = RF – EF

If the reflflector is stationary, DF = 0. If the blood flflow approaches the transducer, DF> 0 and if the flflow moves away from the transducer, DF<0 (fifigure 34). DF is directly proportional to the flflow velocity.

Recording the DF variation as a func tion of time represents the basic information obtained by Doppler exa­

mination. Under optimal conditions of examination, the Doppler method records the variation in speed and direction of blood flflow as a function of time.

Doppler shift has the order of magnitude kHz, falling within the audible range. For this reason, the Doppler signal has both a graphical representation and an audio correspondent.

For a good quality Doppler examination, it is necessary that:

  • the angle between the US beam and the direction of flflow in the vessel is as small as possible and
  • the emitted US frequency is as low as possible.

Simultaneously performing a two-dimensional ultrasound and a high-quality Doppler examination is diffificult due to the two methods’ antagonistic physical requirements. 38 l I. INTRODUCTORY NOTIONS

5.7.3. Information obtained using the Doppler method

The information obtained by the Doppler method is recorded on a graph that represents the variation of the differential frequency as a function of time and is called the Doppler trace (or Doppler signal) (fifigure 35). This graph represents the flflow velocity vertically (or, optionally, DF) and horizontally, the time. All oblique tracings defifine the change of speed over time: increase (acceleration) or decrease (deceleration). The primary information the Doppler effect to study the blood flflow. Details in provided by the Doppler method about the blood flflow are:

  • presence,
  • direction,
  • the speed and character of the blood flflow and the estimation of the number of red blood cells that contribute to the genesis of the Doppler signal.

High diagnostic value secondary in­ formation may be derived from the primary information, such as the pressure gradient between the two sides of a stenosis or a valve orififice, severity of arterial stenosis, blood flflow volume through a vessel, etc.

5.7.4. Modalities of examining and recording Doppler information

There are four main Doppler examination techniques: continuous, pulsed, color and power. Pulsed and color Doppler methods are the most useful, but continuous and power techniques have specifific indications.

5.7.4.1. Continuous emission Doppler

examination. For this examination, the transducer consists of two adjacent piezoelectric crystals, one of which emits the US continuously and the other one continuously receives the echoes.

This technique’s main advantage is that the transducer is small in size and allows easy examination of peripheral vessels. Also, this type of equipment has a relatively low cost. The disadvantages of this technique arise from the fact that it has no spatial resolution.

examination (pulsed Doppler). This examination mode’s characteristic is that the

In this way, one can study blood flflow behavior in a minimal area of the body without the neighboring bloodstream’s inflfluence. (fifigure 36).

The information obtained by the pulsed Doppler method can be represented both graphically and aurally. The pulsed Doppler curve has a similar appearance to that obtained by directional Doppler with continuous emission. Since the US emission is pulsed, the two-dimensional ultrasound image obtained almost simultaneously with the Doppler signal is used to select the sample’s location. 6.1. Computer tomography: physics aspects

Computer tomography (CT) scanning is a type of diagnostic imaging procedure that involves the indirect measurement of the attenuation of X-rays at numerous positions located around the studied object. As a fundamental principle, the density of tissues the X-ray beam passes through can be measured by calculating the attenuation coeffificient.

The amount of attenuation is determined by the imaged tissue’s density, and they are individually assigned a Hounsfifield Unit (HU) or CT number.

The image is acquired using CT slices oriented perpendicular to the body’s longitudinal axis and named axial or transverse sections. For each section, the X-ray tube rotates around the patient to obtain a preselected section thickness.

The CT system employs a continuous rotation and fan-beam design: the X-ray tube and detector are coupled and rotate continuously around the scan fifield while X-rays are emitted and detected. After passing through the body, the X-rays reach the detectors on the opposite side of the patient (fifigure 39).

Spiral (helical) CT allows the entire body to be imaged in a few seconds, with volumetric scan data acquisition.

Multidetector CT (MDCT) scanners have multiple parallel rows of X-ray detectors (an ever-increasing number, now exceeding 250 in some scanners, and capable of reconstructing more than 500 slices at a time). With MDCT, each of the detector

6.2. Scanning protocols – general principles

The specifific CT protocols used for various body segments depend on the scanner used, the scanner manufacturer and the study’s purpose. However, several general principles apply to all CT scans.

Scan levels: while the patient table is moving continuously through the gantry, a digital radiograph (“scout view”) is produced. On this, the volume needed to cover the desired body segment is determined.

Patient position: routinely, patients are scanned supine. Prone scans may be obtained to assess pleural flfluid collection movement, for biopsy procedures or drainage of pleural flfluid collections.

Scanning and patient’s breathing:

scans are routinely obtained after a full inspiration and during suspended respiration to reduce motion artifacts.

Detector row and slice thickness:

scan data are usually acquired with the thinnest detector width available on the scanner (detector rows on most scanners range from 0.25 to 0.625 mm). The indication for the scan determines the reconstructed slice thickness used for scan interpretation. Thin slices are required for specifific indications, whereas thicker slices are quicker to interpret and do not occupy as much memory when stored.

Pitch (table excursion). The term pitch refers to the distance the table travels during a complete gantry rotation divided by the width of all the detectors used (e.g., table excursion/detector width x number of detector rows). Spatial resolution is slightly reduced and the effective slice thickness (the thickness of the slice through the patient that is imaged) is increased.

Scan duration: a MDCT exam can be easily performed during a single breathhold, generally avoiding motion artifacts (respiratory, heart movement, peristalsis), except in very dyspneic or uncooperative patients.

Partial volume effects: the radiologist determines the thickness of the image. Therefore, a structure may be included in the entire thickness of a slice or only in a part of it. Partial volume effects occur when structures do not occupy the entire thickness of a slice.

Reconstruction algorithm: once the scans have been performed, the scan data are reconstructed using an algorithm that determines the resulting image’s characteristics. For routine chest imaging, a high-resolution algorithm is often used to optimize details, but this makes the image somewhat noisy in appearance. A standard or soft-tissue algorithm, which produces a smoother image, is better for assessing thoracic and abdominal vascular structures (e.g., studies performed to diagnose pulmonary embolism, aneurysm, or aortic dissection) but is not optimal for other chest imaging purposes.

Two­ and three­dimensional re­

construction: as the scan data are acquired continuously and volumetrically by spiral CT, scans may be reconstructed in any desired plane. Various display techniques have been used: multiplanar reconstructions, three-dimensional shaded surface display or volume rendering from an external perspective, or shaded surface or volume rendering from an internal (i.e., endoluminal) perspective, also known as virtual bronchoscopy or virtual colonoscopy.

6.5. Radiation dose with CT

Medical radiation results in a defifinite risk, although the patient risk from radiation exposure during diagnostic CT is small and diffificult to determine.

In clinical practice, the patient’s potential benefifits from a CT study need to be balanced against the small radiation risk. In general, if the study has well-defifined clinical utility, it is indicated. The radiologist needs to reduce radiation exposure during diagnostic CT, as long as crucial diagnostic information is not compromised.

The effective dose (measured in sieverts or, more typically, millisieverts) is determined by summing the absorbed doses of individual organs weighted for the irradiation sensitivity and represents the most widely used method for quantifying the radiation dose and comparison of radiologic procedures.

7.6. MRI hardware

As shown so far, MR imaging is based on the successive activation and deactivation of some magnets. Although permanent magnets (like those on the refrigerator) have been used in the past, most present-day MRI scanners employ electromagnets to create the magnetic fifields. An electromagnet is composed of a coil (loop) of wire that behaves like a magnet when an electric current passes through it. There are three types of magnets incorporated in the hull of the tunnel-shaped MRI scanner.

The primary electromagnet is always turned on and creates the main (B0) longitudinalmagneticfifieldwithanintensityof 1,5or 3 Tesla (Earth’s magnetic fifield at the surface has an intensity of 25-65 *10−6Tesla). The primary magnet is composed of a niobium alloy coil kept at a constant temperature close to absolute 0 (usually between -269 and -265°C). The coil maintained at such a 58 l I. INTRODUCTORY NOTIONS low temperature acts as a superconductor, which means that the electric current will circulate through the coil indefifinitely even after being disconnected from the power source. To keep the temperature constant, the superconducting coil is located within a thermally insulated cryostat fifilled with liquid helium. As the helium heats up, it evaporates and must be captured and compressed back into its liquid state using a continuously working pump that one hears in all modern MRI scanner rooms.

The gradient coils generate the three perpendicular gradient magnetic fifields necessary for spatial localization: the sliceselect gradient, the phase encoding gradient and the frequency encoding gradient. The gradient coils are made out of resistive electromagnets that need to be connected to a power source to generate a magnetic fifield; therefore, they can be quickly turned on and off. The loud banging noise specifific for MRI scanners occurs when the gradient magnets try to align to the main longitudinal magnetic fifield as they are turned on but are held in place by their mountings, exerting stress on them.

The radiofrequency (RF) coil is also a resistive electromagnet that can be quickly turned on and off and is responsible for generating the rotating magnetic fifield (RF pulse) that excites the protons. It is called radiofrequency fifield because it rotates at the frequency ω0, which happens to be in the range of radio waves.

The receiver coil (antenna) is used for detecting the transverse magnetic fifield (signal) originating within the patient. This signal carries the useful data necessary for MR imaging. When the antenna is exposed to a transverse magnetic fifield, an electric current starts flflowing through its coil, which can be detected by a voltmeter and then analyzed by a computer (fifigure 56). The magnetic fifield can accelerate ferromagnetic objects at very high speeds towards the MRI scanner, potentially harming patients or staff in their way. There have been reports of objects such as oxygen tanks, chairs, and beds projected inside the scanner room, with at least one death caused this way. A thorough screening of patients and staff entering the scanner room must be made to prevent such incidents, and unauthorized personnel’s access must be restricted. 62 l I. INTRODUCTORY NOTIONS

7.8.2. Adverse effects caused by implants

Before entering the scanner room, patients are asked regarding any medical or non-medical implants they might have in their bodies. Depending on their location, non-medical ferromagnetic foreign objects can prove dangerous due to their risk of dislodgement. For example, a bullet or metal splinter close to important blood vessels or a metal splinter in the eye can represent absolute contraindications. Medical implants are classifified as active or non-active, depending on the presence of a power source.

Active implantable devices are defifined as devices that need an energy source to function: pacemakers, defifibrillators, neurostimulators, cochlear implants and drug pumps. These implants can be dislodged, damaged by the magnetic fifield, losing their function and can overheat, causing burns. The malfunction of such devices can be life-threatening, as is the case with defifibrillators and pacemakers. Some newer active implants have been designed to be MR safe or MR conditional and can be safely used in an MRI environment. However, any unlabeled device or a device for which a document certifying its safety can not be provided must be considered MR unsafe.

Non-active implantable medical devices are defifined as implants that do not require a power source to function: orthopedic implants, heart valves, stents, aneurysm clips, etc. Modern orthopedic implants are considered safe as the magnetic fifield can not dislodge them. In the rare instances when they overheat and discomfort is experienced, the MRI exposure can be discontinued. Heart valves, intravascular stents, fifilters and coils are also considered MRI safe. In the case of cardiac valvular implants, it has been demonstrated that the forces exerted by the normal motion of the heart are higher than those caused by magnetic attraction. It is essential for all these implants to wait 6-8 weeks after implantation for them to be securely attached in place by fifibrous proliferation. Intracranial aneurysm clips pose a particular danger as they are not always held in place by fifibrotic tissue and can be dislodged under the inflfluence of the magnetic fifield. These clips must be considered unsafe unless they are documented to be non-ferromagnetic.

7.8.3. Heating

The excitation of the protons using the RF coils is a means of energy transfer from the MRI scanner to the patient leading to diffuse heating. This is quantifified using the specifific absorption rate (SAR) and regulations were established to limit energy deposition not to overheat the patients. An increase in body core temperature of less than 1°C should not adversely affect the general population. In children and patients with cardiovascular pathology, that limit should not exceed 0.5° C. Some MRI scanners automatically abort the scan if a dangerous SAR threshold has been exceeded.

7.8.4. Burns

Contact burns are caused by the proximity between the patient and metallic objects that can overheat during the RF pulse. Such objects can be ECG connectors, pulse oximeters, transdermal medicinal patches, clothing containing metal wire, and even coil cables. Care must be taken to avoid direct contact of such objects with the skin and adequate insulation is used. Moreover, wires that need to be placed on the patient should not form any loops, as this confifiguration is more likely to overheat. Tattoos containing pigment can overheat, although usually not enough to cause burns. Facial make-up can also overheat, so prior removal is advised.

Induced current burns are caused when the patient’s body parts create a conductive loop. For instance, keeping the legs or the arms crossed, or even the bare thighs in contact with each other can cause burns. It is important to note that temperatures as low as 43°C can cause burns, and the patient will not initially sense any pain. For this reason, the patient should be positioned with care and instructed not to change that position. Although contact and induced current burns are very rare, they can occasionally induce severe burns.

7.8.5. Stimulation of peripheral nerves

The exposure to the alternating gradient of magnetic fifields can induce neurostimulation, especially of the peripheral nerves in the arms and legs. The effects are very variable, ranging from slight discomfort to pain and induction of muscle contractions. Neurostimulation occurs rarely and some patients might be more sensitive than others.

7.8.6. Acoustic injury

The noises caused by the gradient magnetic fifield’s successive activation and deactivation can reach up to 130 dB. Loud noises can be harmful to the eardrum, cases of temporary hearing loss due to unprotected sound exposure in MRI scanners having been reported. For this reason, patients are routinely offered headphones that signifificantly reduce noise exposure and can be used to communicate instructions to the patient.

7.8.7. Claustrophobia and sedation

Some patients become claustrophobic when entering the narrow MRI bore and often want to interrupt the exam. Talking

7. MRI PHYSICS l 63 and reassuring the patient before and during the procedure may prevent this. Allowing a companion to stay with the patient in the scanner room may also be helpful. The use of open MRI scanners can be useful, but few hospitals own such devices. All patients in the scanner have a panic button at their disposal, allowing them to alert the staff if needed. If other means are not successful, sedation under the supervision of an anesthesiologist might be necessary. Sedation is also necessary for children who need to undergo MRI examinations and are too young to follow instructions.

7.8.8. MRI in pregnancy

Studies on animal models have shown growth delay and malformations in fetuses exposed to strong magnetic fifields, which have raised concerns about humans’ similar effects. However, these results can not be directly extrapolated for humans and the human studies published so far have shown no adverse effects. For this reason, currently, no defifinitive data is confifirming or dismissing potential harm caused by MRI magnetic fifields to the fetus. MRI is considered to be safe for the evaluation of fetal malformations after 18 weeks of gestation. Before 18 weeks, MRI scans should be recommended with caution only if the advantages outweigh the potential adverse effects. Pregnant staff can safely work in the MRI environment as long as they exit the MRI room while scanning.

    8.3. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)

    The measurement of the signal re-emitted by an atom such as hydrogen, the main constituent of the human body, makes it possible to determine the explored tissue’s chemical composition after stopping the radiofrequency wave application.

    The natural contrast of the tissues is much greater than that of a CT scan.

    The magnetic fifield (B0) of the gantry and the radio frequency wave (B1) represent the image’s source. The magnet is responsible for B0. The coil produces the RF wave. The antennas (coils) are chosen according to the part of the body (“knee” antenna, “skull” antenna, etc.), being responsible for emitting and then receiving the signal.

    Image type: imaging of any part of the body can be obtained in any plane - in axial (transversal), frontal (coronal), sagittal, oblique or volumetric acquisitions.
